goal: Someone who meets the product for the first time starts using it, from the README alone, only when it serves their work.

user_benefits.what: Asked by a colleague what the product is, does the reader answer in one sentence that tells what it does?
Reading the gain, does the reader tell what the product would let them do, and so whether it is for them?
Weighing the product against what they would do without it, does the reader see the problem that way leaves them with, and what the product does instead?
Before installing, does the reader see what the product does not do that they might expect of it?
Before installing, does the reader see where the product is not yet fit for use?
After the walkthrough, does the reader see that the product would give them, on work of their own, the gain the opening promised?
Starting with nothing set up, does the reader install the product by the README's steps alone, and see that it works?
Looking at how the product works, does the reader see how it keeps each gain and makes each condition behind the opening's problem hold?
Needing more than the README gives, such as fuller use or help, does the reader find where to go next?
Weighing whether they may use the product, does the reader find the terms for them and their team?
Reading from the top, does the reader find each answer just when they come to need it, so they can stop once they have what they came for?

practices.thinking: Write one sentence on its own line under the title that names the kind of thing the product is and what it does, in words the reader already uses and with no feature name or mechanism, as the reader then can say it again to a colleague.
steps: Where a colleague who hears only the sentence could not say what the product does, replace each vague or praising word with what it does.

practices.thinking: Name whom the product is for by the work they want done, and the gain as what they can then do, taken from the objectives of the product's UX, as the reader tells from it whether the product meets their need.
steps: Where a reader outside that group could not tell from it that the product is not for them, name the group and the work more closely.

practices.thinking: Say in a few plain sentences the problem that what the reader would do without the product leaves them with, and in one sentence the product's idea, as the reader decides by a problem they know as their own, while how the product removes it is left to How it works.
steps: Take the reader's problem from the objectives of the product's UX: what keeps the role from what its objective says.
Find the usual way in what the reader would do if the product did not exist, doing nothing among it.

List every condition that must hold for the problem to be solved, by whatever way, from each way the objective fails, such as what its key results count against it; keep one only if a way that misses it leaves the problem unsolved.

For each condition, find where the usual way falls short of it, and leave out a condition it meets, as that gives the reader no reason to choose. For each, find what the product does that makes it hold, from the design. The conditions feed the problem here and How it works, and the opening does not go through them.
Ask the user each condition, and each shortfall of the usual way, that the design does not settle.
From the shortfalls, say the problem as what happens to the reader the usual way, in a few plain sentences in their words, not as how the product works.
Say the idea in one sentence: what the product does differently that removes the problem.

Read the opening as a newcomer deciding whether the product is for them. Cut or reword what they would stumble on, replace each word that only praises with what the product does, and leave how it works to How it works.

practices.thinking: List only what a reader could reasonably expect of the product and it does not do, as a reader who needs it then learns that before they install.
steps: Gather what readers might expect from similar products and from what readers ask, and ask the user whether each is in or out.

practices.thinking: Where the product is not yet fit for use, such as a release still in development or one no longer kept up, say so at the top, as a reader who starts on it otherwise finds out only once their work rests on it.
Show one real run of the use most readers come for, on work like theirs, with the product's real output, as the reader then sees that the product works and what they would get.
steps: Pick the use from what readers ask for most, such as help requests, and from the main scenario of the product's UX.
Say at the start what the reader will have at the end.

Take each exchange, what the user gives and what the product shows, from the record of a real run in the form the reader sees it: text in a code block of its language, and a screen as an image taken from the run, cutting only what the reader does not need to see the result.
Where the result does not show the gain the opening promised, pick another piece of work or another scenario.

practices.thinking: Write the requirements and the install steps for a reader who has nothing set up, and try them that way, as the author's own setup hides the gaps.
steps: Give even a common install step as a command to copy.
From a machine or sandbox where nothing the product needs is in place, follow the steps as written and do nothing they do not say.
Where a step fails, or needs what the README does not say, write it in and start again.

practices.thinking: Draw who does what to whom so that each gain holds and each condition behind the opening's problem is met, and say under it how each condition is met, in as much detail as a reader new to the product can follow, as a reader trusts a promise they see kept.
steps: Take each condition, where the usual way falls short of it and what the product does, from the design, as Q3 digs them.
Point to each gain and each condition, and find the lines of the figure that make it hold. Where none does, mend the figure or the promise.

Under the figure, say for each condition in a sentence or two, in the reader's words, how the parts of the figure make it hold. Never sort the conditions in a table, as a table is how the developer sorts them, while the reader needs to see what happens.
Leave each non-goal to the opening, as a figure shows what the product does.

practices.thinking: Keep in the README what the reader needs to decide and to start, and link one place for each need that comes after, such as fuller use or help, as a README that holds everything is not read.
steps: Open each link.

practices.thinking: Name the license and link its full text, as a reader may rule the product out by its license alone.
steps: Open the link, and check that it reaches the license the name says.

practices.thinking: Order the README as the reader decides, from what every reader needs to what only a reader who has chosen the product needs, as each reader then stops once they have what they came for.
steps: Read the README from the top as someone who meets the product for the first time, and after each section, write the question the reader now has.
Check that the next part answers that question. Move a section that answers a later one.
Cut what no reader needs at the point where it stands, or move it to the document a link leads to.
